question.problem: What is the last digit in the decimal expansion of ${14}^{14}?$
question.worked_solution:
If $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ and $c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

- $ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- ${a}^{k}≡{b}^{k}\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue:

$$
{14}^{14}\text{ mod }10
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & ≡10+4\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{14}^{2} & ≡{4}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡16\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡10+6\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡0+6\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {14}^{6} & ≡{({14}^{2})}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡{6}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡216\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡21\cdot 10+6 & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡21\cdot 0+6 & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we decompose ${14}^{14}$ into a product of smaller exponents. 

$$
{14}^{14}={({14}^{6})}^{2}\cdot {14}^{2}
$$

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{14}^{14} & ≡{({14}^{6})}^{2}\cdot {14}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡(6)^{2}\cdot 6\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡216\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡21\cdot 10+6\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡21\cdot 0+6 & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{14}^{14}\text{ mod }10=6
$$

which means that the last digit of ${14}^{14}$ is $6.$
